title: Ticket Booking
subtitle: Ticketmaster / BookMyShow Architecture: Virtual Waiting Room, Temporary Seat Holds, OCC & Flash-Sale Stampede Defense
keyTakeaways: Prevent double-booking using a Two-Phase Seat Reservation pattern: Phase 1 acquires an atomic 10-minute temporary hold (`AVAILABLE -> HELD`) using Redis Lua / DB Optimistic Concurrency Control (`version` check), and Phase 2 transitions `HELD -> BOOKED` upon payment completion.

Protect the core booking database during celebrity concert drops (e.g., Taylor Swift / Coldplay with 5M concurrent fans for 50,000 seats) using an Edge Virtual Waiting Room (Queue-it style token bucket) that admits users into the seat-map checkout at a controlled rate.

Never rely solely on a Redis TTL expiration event to release abandoned holds: store `hold_expires_at` directly in the database seat row so any query or CAS update treats an expired `HELD` seat (`hold_expires_at < NOW()`) as immediately bookable.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A Ticket Booking platform (like Ticketmaster, BookMyShow, or StubHub) sells assigned seats for concerts, sports games, and movie screenings. The defining challenge is surviving extreme flash-sale traffic spikes while guaranteeing zero double-booked seats.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Users can browse events, venues, and real-time interactive seat maps (`AVAILABLE`, `HELD`, `BOOKED`); (2) Users can select up to 6 specific seats (or request 'Best Available' contiguous seats) and lock them for a 10-minute checkout window; (3) If payment succeeds within 10 minutes, the seats transition to `BOOKED` and an e-ticket QR code is issued; (4) If payment fails or the 10-minute timer expires, the seats automatically return to `AVAILABLE`; (5) Fair admission during high-demand drops via a Virtual Waiting Room.

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Consistency: Strict strong consistency on seat reservations—**zero double booking** under any concurrency scenario; (2) Availability: 99.99% for event browsing and waiting room admission; (3) Latency: P99 < 100ms for loading the venue seat map, P99 < 200ms for acquiring a seat hold; (4) Surge Isolation: A flash sale on 1 hot concert must not degrade movie ticket bookings across the rest of the platform.
Out of Scope: Secondary peer-to-peer ticket resale marketplace, dynamic airline yield pricing algorithms, and venue turnstile hardware firmware.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: Normal daily traffic is modest, but flash sales create a 100x–500x hotspot on a single `show_id` within a 60-second window.
bullets: Platform Baseline: 50 Million DAU browsing events; 3 Million tickets booked per day across 100,000 active shows (movies, concerts, sports).
Seat Inventory per Show: Movie theater = 300 seats; Arena concert = 20,000 seats; Stadium concert = 80,000 seats.
Flash Sale Hotspot Traffic: 5 Million concurrent users attempting to buy 80,000 seats for a single stadium concert at 10:00:00 AM.
Read Traffic: 500 Million seat-map views/day baseline (~5,800 QPS avg); during a flash sale, 5M users polling or connected via SSE = up to 500,000 seat-map reads/sec.

Write Traffic (Hold + Book): Baseline 3M bookings/day ≈ 35 bookings/sec; during a flash sale, the Virtual Waiting Room throttles active checkout admissions to 10,000 concurrent users -> ~5,000 seat-hold attempts/sec against the hot show.
Payload Sizes: Seat row in DB = 128 bytes; Compact Seat Map Status payload for an 80,000-seat stadium (2 bits per seat: `00`=Available, `01`=Held, `10`=Booked) = 20 KB compressed.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Because the total number of active seats across all upcoming shows is surprisingly small, the entire global seat inventory easily fits in memory!
bullets: Baseline & Flash-Sale Read QPS: 5,800 QPS average; 500,000 QPS peak during stadium drops (served via Edge CDN + Redis Bitfield/Hash cache).
Baseline & Flash-Sale Write QPS: 70 writes/sec average (Hold + Confirm); 10,000 writes/sec peak (throttled by Virtual Waiting Room pass verification).

Redis Memory (Active Show Seat Maps + Waiting Room Queues): (a) 100,000 active shows × average 2,000 seats × 64 bytes per seat in Redis = 12.8 GB! Even 1,000 stadium shows (80,000 seats each) take only 5.1 GB; (b) Virtual Waiting Room queues for 10M queued users × 64 bytes = 640 MB. A 64 GB Redis cluster holds every active seat on Earth in RAM.

5-Year Relational Storage (Bookings, Tickets & Historical Shows): 100,000 shows/day × 2,000 seats × 128 bytes = 25.6 GB/day + 3M bookings/day × 1 KB = 3 GB/day -> ~28.6 GB/day -> 10.4 TB/year -> 52.2 TB over 5 years. With 3x replication and indexes ≈ 200 TB.

Bandwidth: Peak Egress during flash sale = 500,000 seat-map reads/sec × 20 KB (compact bitfield/section JSON) = 10 GB/sec (80 Gbps, 95% offloaded by 1-second micro-caching at CDN/Edge + WebSocket delta pushes).

codeSnippet.title: Ticket Booking Capacity & Flash-Sale Sizing Worksheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
TICKET BOOKING CAPACITY WORKSHEET (3M TICKETS/DAY + 5M USER FLASH SALE)
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT (BASELINE vs. STADIUM FLASH SALE)
   - Avg Seat-Map Read QPS    : 500,000,000 / 86,400        = 5,787 QPS
   - Flash-Sale Read QPS      : 5M users / 10s refresh      = 500,000 QPS
   - Avg Booking Write QPS    : 3,000,000 * 2 / 86,400      = 69 QPS
   - Flash-Sale Hold Write QPS: Throttled by Waiting Room   = 10,000 QPS

2. REDIS MEMORY (100% OF ACTIVE SEAT INVENTORY IN RAM)
   - Active Shows (100K)      : 100,000 shows * 2,000 seats = 200,000,000 seats
   - Per-Seat Cache Entry     : 64 bytes                    = 12.8 GB
   - Waiting Room ZSETs (10M) : 10,000,000 users * 64 bytes = 640 MB
   - Total Redis Cluster (2x) : ~13.5 GB * 2 (Replica)      = 27.0 GB RAM

3. 5-YEAR ACID DATABASE STORAGE
   - Daily Show Seat Rows     : 200M seats * 128 B          = 25.6 GB / day
   - Daily Booking Orders     : 3M orders * 1 KB            = 3.0 GB / day
   - 5-Year Raw Storage       : 28.6 GB * 365 * 5           = 52.2 TB
   - 3x Replicated + Indexes  : 52.2 TB * 3 * 1.3           = 203.6 TB

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH (STADIUM SEAT MAP = 80,000 SEATS)
   - Compact Seat Bitmap Size : 80,000 seats * 2 bits       = 20 KB
   - Peak Egress (500K QPS)   : 500,000 * 20 KB             = 10.0 GB/s (80 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Design & Entities (with Entity Diagram)
sections.body: Core external REST/gRPC/WebSocket API contracts, request/response payloads, and underlying storage entities with primary keys (PK), foreign keys (FK), secondary/clustering indexes (IDX), and relationship cardinalities.
bullets: GET /api/v1/shows/{showId}/seat-map — Returns compressed seat availability bitmask/hash from Redis cache.
POST /api/v1/shows/{showId}/holds — Atomically places a 7-minute temporary hold on selected seats using OCC version check.
POST /api/v1/bookings/{bookingId}/confirm — Finalizes seat status from HELD to BOOKED upon payment verification.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture uses a two-layer defense: an Edge Virtual Waiting Room to shape incoming flash-sale traffic, and a Redis + PostgreSQL/CockroachDB core partitioned by `show_id` to guarantee atomic multi-seat holds.
bullets: Edge Virtual Waiting Room (Cloudflare Workers + Redis ZSET): When a hot concert goes on sale, users join a virtual waiting room. At 10:00 AM, users are assigned a randomized queue position and popped in batches of 2,000/sec. Admitted users receive an HMAC-signed JWT `X-Queue-Pass-Token` valid for 15 minutes.

Seat Map Query Service & Compact Bitmap Cache: Serves the 80,000-seat stadium map from Redis and pushes real-time seat status diffs (`seatId: HELD`) over WebSockets/SSE to users currently viewing that stadium section.

Booking Service: Validates the `X-Queue-Pass-Token`, executes an atomic multi-seat hold in Redis via a Lua script (fast-fail gatekeeper), and commits the authoritative `AVAILABLE -> HELD` state transition in the relational database using OCC (`version` + lazy `hold_expires_at` check).

Hold Expiration Sweeper & Payment Webhook Listener: Confirms `HELD -> BOOKED` upon payment capture, or sweeps expired `HELD` rows (`hold_expires_at < NOW()`) back to `AVAILABLE` and updates the Redis bitmap.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Below we trace (Flow 1) Two-Phase Atomic Multi-Seat Hold with Lazy Expiration and OCC, and (Flow 2) Virtual Waiting Room Queue Admission & Contiguous 'Best Available' Seat Allocation.
bullets: Flow 1 — Atomic Multi-Seat Hold with Lazy Expiration & OCC: Suppose 1,000 users click seats `[101, 102]` at the exact same millisecond. First, a Redis Lua script checks if `seat:101` and `seat:102` are currently held; 999 requests fail in <0.5ms at the Redis layer without ever touching PostgreSQL. The 1 winning request proceeds to PostgreSQL, sorts the seat IDs `[101, 102]`, and executes an atomic update that succeeds *either* if `status = 'AVAILABLE'` *or* if `status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < NOW()` (Lazy Expiration!). This means even if a background cron job is delayed by 30 seconds, an expired seat hold is immediately bookable the exact millisecond `hold_expires_at` passes.

Flow 2 — Virtual Waiting Room & 'Best Available' Bitmask Search: For mega-events, showing a clickable 80,000-seat map causes severe contention because thousands of fans click the exact same front-row seats. Instead, the UI switches to 'Section / Best Available' mode: the user asks for `N = 4` contiguous seats in `Section 102`. The Booking Service represents each row of 32 seats as a 32-bit integer bitmask in memory (`0` = available, `1` = taken) and finds `N` adjacent available seats in $O(1)$ CPU cycles using bitwise shifts (`mask & (mask << 1) & (mask << 2) & (mask << 3)`).

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To survive extreme celebrity ticket drops and bot armies, production ticketing platforms add edge bot mitigation, anti-scalping cryptographic tickets, and dynamic UI degradation.
bullets: Lazy Expiration + Background Sweeper Dual Defense: Relying *only* on a background cron job to flip expired `HELD` rows back to `AVAILABLE` introduces a window where seats appear unavailable after 10 minutes if the cron lags. Relying *only* on lazy expiration leaves the Redis seat-map cache stale until someone clicks that seat. Combine both: the SQL `WHERE` clause checks `hold_expires_at < NOW()` for instant correctness, while a lightweight Sweeper every 5 seconds refreshes the Redis seat-map bitmap for the UI.

Dynamic UI Degradation (Interactive Seat Map -> Section Auto-Assign): When concurrent traffic for a single `show_id` exceeds 50,000 users, disable individual seat clicking on the frontend (which causes 99% OCC collisions on the most popular front-row seats) and switch to 'Select Section & Quantity' mode backed by per-section partitioned queues and bitwise contiguous seat allocation.

Anti-Scalper Bot Defense & Verified Fan Tokens: Require pre-registered 'Verified Fan' cryptographic tokens before entering the Virtual Waiting Room, combined with proof-of-work challenges and device attestation at the CDN edge so headless scripts cannot exhaust the 10-minute seat hold pool.

Rotating TOTP Dynamic QR Codes for Venue Entry: Static PDF barcodes are easily screenshotted and resold to multiple buyers. Issue tickets as a seed secret inside the mobile app that renders a rotating 15-second TOTP barcode (`HMAC-SHA256(ticketSecret, currentEpoch / 15)`), eliminating screenshot fraud at the stadium gates.

tradeOffs.option: Pessimistic Locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) vs. Optimistic Concurrency Control (`version` column)
tradeOffs.pros: Pessimistic locking serializes conflicting transactions inside the DB engine without throwing immediate retry errors.
tradeOffs.cons: Under a flash sale where 5,000 users target the same seat row, waiting on row locks ties up all database connections and causes cascading thread-pool exhaustion.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-contention back-office updates; for high-contention ticket drops, Redis fast-fail gatekeeping + DB OCC (`version` check) is far more resilient.

tradeOffs.option: Interactive Seat Map Selection vs. Server-Assigned 'Best Available' Section Allocation
tradeOffs.pros: Interactive Seat Map gives users exact control over aisle/view preferences.
tradeOffs.cons: Causes extreme collision rates during flash sales because thousands of users click the exact same visually prominent seats simultaneously.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Use Interactive Seat Map for movies and regular concerts; dynamically switch to 'Best Available' Section Allocation during stadium flash sales.

tradeOffs.option: Redis-Only Seat Hold vs. Redis Gatekeeper + Durable DB `hold_expires_at`
tradeOffs.pros: Redis-only holds are ultra-fast and expire automatically via Redis TTL.
tradeOffs.cons: If a Redis master crashes before replicating to its replica, two users can hold the same seat and both proceed to payment.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Always pair the Redis Lua gatekeeper with an authoritative ACID database update (`status = 'HELD'`, `hold_expires_at`) before initiating payment.

interviewTip: Be sure to mention **Lazy Expiration** (`WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < NOW())`) and **sorting `seatIds` ascending** before locking multiple seats. Those two details immediately signal to the interviewer that you have built real concurrent reservation systems and know how to prevent both cron-lag unavailability and multi-row deadlocks.
